doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Bay Area youth and early listening
title: Big band music at home, first trombone, and seeing Ellington's band
summary: Turré says jazz had his heart early; his parents met at a Count Basie dance, he watched Dizzy, Bird and Armstrong on TV, started trombone in fourth grade, and was taken to see the real Ellington band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Right. I’m fascinated by the path that notable musicians take. And I was thinking about the fact that if I’m correct, you grew up, your formative years when you might have been most affected by what you heard were in the San Francisco area?

In the mid-60s, there was so much music going on in the pop world and in the jazz world, and you were in an area known for innovations in rock music. And I wonder if there was a time when you considered that music as a career?

Not as a career, no. But I enjoyed it and I played it too, but you know jazz had my heart from an early age, early age. You know my mom and dad met at a Count Basie dance. And we had big band music, that was the dance music of their day you know. So you know we had big band music in the house all the time and I used to watch the Ed Sullivan Show and I saw Dizzy and Bird on there, I saw Louis Armstrong many times, as well as all the other great R&B and pop acts too. So I enjoyed all kinds of music. They had Nat Cole’s show and all that, so I saw all that stuff coming up in the late 50s. And then in the 60s you know I would start playing trombone in the fourth grade. And then in middle school, which was sixth, seventh, eighth, they had a jazz band and that’s when I started playing jazz. And this was before I started hearing pop and rock and funk. And then in high school, well actually I’m going to go back a bit. When I first started playing trombone in the fourth grade my parents took me to the Oakland Auditorium to see Duke Ellington. Not a ghost band, the real Duke Ellington. And Coleman Hawkins was the guest soloist, Ella Fitzgerald was a guest vocalist, Clark Terry was in the band, Johnny Hodges, Britt Woodman was playing lead trombone. He took Lawrence Brown’s place and he later played with me on a couple of my records. And there’s a lot of connections. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
